*Thinking as the farmer, in her own voice:*

Aiya, another season. My back isn't what it was but the fields don't farm themselves. My husband — gone seven years now — and my eldest son works at the brick plant in town, only home on weekends. So it's mostly me, and my daughter-in-law when the grandchildren let her.

Ten mu and a bit. I've done wheat-maize on the big piece as long as I can remember, ever since the land was divided up. Keeps us in flour, keeps the chickens fed, and the straw for the stove. The west patch, the sandy one, I put to cotton — my old man started that back when the price was good, and I still do maybe three mu. One lump of cash when we sell it to the buyer in autumn. I thought about dropping the cotton — picking kills my back — but the ginners still come round and my daughter-in-law helps.

**For the wheat** (seven mu) — I plant right after National Day cools off, around the tenth of October. I saved a sack of seed from last year like always, the Jimai kind my nephew got me a few years back, still works fine. Before planting I spread two bags of compound fertilizer — the blue-bag kind, 15-15-15 — across the wheat ground. Then in spring, when it greens up after the New Year, I scatter urea, about one bag for every three mu. If it looks yellow at jointing I'll put a bit more. Water — I run the well once before winter, once at green-up, once at jointing. Every time I turn that electric pump on that's yuan gone, so I don't do it unless the ground cracks. Four times if it's a dry spring. I hire the combine to cut it in June; 80 yuan a mu, everyone pays the same.

**For the maize** — goes straight into the wheat ground the same week the combine leaves. Tight — my son comes home for three days to help. I pay the planter driver to put down compound fertilizer with the seed, that saves a pass. About a month later, when the maize is up to my knee, I scatter urea down the rows. One time, maybe two, for water if July is dry — usually the summer rain carries it. Harvest by hand end of September, hang the ears under the eaves to dry.

**For the cotton** (three mu, west plot) — plant end of April when the ground warms. Cotton's hungry, I put a full ration of compound when I make the ridges. Spray for bollworm two, three times in summer, my son picks up the spray from the shop in town. One water before flowering if it's dry. Picking starts September and drags into October — my daughter-in-law helps, and I hire two neighbor women for about a week when the bolls are all open.

I don't spend money I don't have. If a year goes bad I still have wheat in the sack. That's how it's always been.
